prompt: Why does a replica set have three members rather than two?

choices.text: So that any two of them are a majority that can still decide
choices.why: Right. With two, a member that loses its partner cannot tell a crash from a cut cable, and one of two is not a majority.

choices.text: So that reads can be spread over three machines
choices.why: Reads go to the primary by default; the number three is about deciding, not about load.

choices.text: Because each member stores a third of the data
choices.why: Every member holds all of it. Splitting the data is sharding, lesson 10.

choices.text: Because MongoDB refuses to start a set of two members at all
choices.why: It allows it; it simply cannot survive losing either member.

prompt: The three containers were started with `--bind_ip_all`. What would happen without it?

choices.text: Each `mongod` would listen only on `127.0.0.1`, and the other members could not reach it
choices.why: Right. Listening on localhost alone is the default, and a replica set talks over the network.

choices.text: The containers would become reachable from the internet through the VM's own address
choices.why: The option widens what mongod listens on inside the container; no port is published either way.

choices.text: The member names would be container ids
choices.why: That is what `--hostname` prevents.

choices.text: `rs.initiate` would choose the primary at random instead of holding an election
choices.why: The election happens either way; this option is about who can connect.

prompt: Right after `rs.initiate`, the prompt on `mongo1` said `rs0 [direct: secondary]`. A moment later it said `primary`. What happened in between?

choices.text: Every member starts as a secondary; `mongo1` won the first election
choices.why: Right. Nobody is primary by being named first; the set elects one.

choices.text: `mongo1` copied the data from the other two before it was allowed to lead
choices.why: There was no data yet, and a primary is not made by copying.

choices.text: `mongosh` silently reconnected to a different container of the set
choices.why: `direct:` means the session stayed on `mongo1` throughout.

choices.text: The prompt was wrong at first and corrected itself
choices.why: It was right both times: the member's state changed.

prompt: What does a secondary copy from the primary?

choices.text: The data files, every few seconds
choices.why: That is the obvious guess, and wrong: files are not shipped.

choices.text: The entries of the oplog, applied in order
choices.why: Right: `local.oplog.rs`, one entry per change.

choices.text: The queries clients sent, which it runs again
choices.why: It copies the changes those queries made, not the queries.

choices.text: Only the documents that clients read from it
choices.why: A secondary copies every change, whether anybody reads it or not.

prompt: With both secondaries frozen, an insert with `w: "majority", wtimeout: 3000` failed with `WriteConcernFailed`. What did `countDocuments()` show next, and why?
hint: Does a write-concern error undo the write?

choices.text: The document was counted: the error is about the confirmation, not the write
choices.why: Right. Three products, the monitor among them. The write sat on the primary with no promise attached.

choices.text: It was not counted, because a failed write is rolled back at once
choices.why: Nothing is undone by a write-concern error; that is what makes a blind retry dangerous.

choices.text: It was counted twice, once per attempt
choices.why: There was one attempt; the shell did not retry.

choices.text: The count failed too, since the secondaries were locked
choices.why: Reads on the primary are not affected by locks on the secondaries.

prompt: Nobody ever set a write concern on the lab's replica set. What does a plain `insertOne` wait for?

choices.text: The primary alone
choices.why: That was the default before MongoDB 5.0. The capture shows `majority`.

choices.text: A majority of the members, with no time limit
choices.why: Right: `{ w: 'majority', wtimeout: 0 }`, source `implicit`.

choices.text: All three members, for at most three seconds each time
choices.why: Three seconds was the `wtimeout` the lesson chose for one insert; the default waits for a majority with no limit.

choices.text: Nothing: an unset write concern is not acknowledged
choices.why: Unacknowledged writes need `w: 0`, asked for explicitly.

prompt: The oplog is a ___ collection: it has a fixed size, and the oldest entries are overwritten as new ones arrive.
hint: One word, the English name for this kind of collection.

prompt: In the capture, `mongo2` was killed at 07:55:23.101 and `mongo3` was elected at 07:55:31.752. For how many seconds was there no primary? Answer to two decimal places.
A planned `docker stop` of the primary produced a new primary in milliseconds; `docker kill` took about nine seconds. What explains the difference?

choices.text: A stopping primary hands over at once; a killed one goes silent, and the others wait out the timeout
choices.why: Right: `stepUpRequestSkipDryRun` against `electionTimeout`.

choices.text: `docker kill` also damaged the data files, and the surviving secondaries had to check them before electing anyone
choices.why: The secondaries never read the dead member's files; they only noticed its silence.

choices.text: A killed container takes longer to release its network name
choices.why: Names have nothing to do with it; the delay is a timeout the members wait out.

choices.text: There was no difference in the server; the shell was slower the second time
choices.why: The timestamps come from the servers themselves.

prompt: A team lowers `electionTimeoutMillis` from ten seconds to one, to make failover faster. What new failure do they invite?
hint: What else, besides a crash, makes heartbeats go unanswered for a second?

choices.text: Writes with `w: 1` stop being acknowledged
choices.why: Write concern is unaffected by the timeout.

choices.text: Elections nobody needed, every time the network pauses briefly
choices.why: Right. A short pause looks like a crash, and each needless election is its own moment with no primary.

choices.text: The secondaries can no longer read the oplog
choices.why: Replication does not depend on the election timeout.

choices.text: A crashed primary returns as primary, since its term has not expired
choices.why: A returning member always rejoins behind the current primary's term.

prompt: When the killed `mongo2` was started again, what state did it come back in?

choices.text: Primary again, because it was primary before it died
choices.why: Nothing in the configuration prefers it, and the set already had a primary.

choices.text: Secondary, catching up from the new primary's oplog
choices.why: Right. `mongo3` stayed primary.

choices.text: Removed from the set until somebody adds it back
choices.why: It is still in the configuration; it simply rejoins.

choices.text: Unreachable, until the whole set is restarted together
choices.why: `rs.status()` showed it healthy as soon as it was up.

prompt: Match each read preference to where a read goes.
hint: One description fits none of them.

pairs.right: the primary, and an error when there is none
a secondary, and the primary only when no secondary answers
whichever member answers fastest, primary or not
the primary, and a secondary only while there is none

right_distractors: every member at once, merging the answers

prompt: With both secondaries frozen, the primary returned 329.90 and a read with `readPref("secondary")` returned 349.90. What told the client that the second answer was old?

choices.text: A warning printed under the result
choices.why: No warning appeared; both reads succeeded quietly.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: Right. A stale read looks exactly like a fresh one; tolerating it is the application's job, lesson 5.

choices.text: An error, because the secondary was locked
choices.why: `fsyncLock` blocks writes on the member, not reads.

choices.text: The prompt changed to `[secondary]` for that line
choices.why: The session stayed connected to the set; the prompt still said `primary`.

prompt: On the primary, with both secondaries frozen, `readConcern("majority")` returned the old price while `"local"` returned the new one. What does this say about `"majority"`?

choices.text: It is buggy on a primary and is meant for secondaries
choices.why: It did exactly what it promises, on the primary.

choices.text: It returns the newest value any member has
choices.why: That is closer to the opposite: the newest value was on one member only.

choices.text: It buys durability, not freshness: it never returns a value that could still be rolled back
choices.why: Right. The new price was on one member of three, so it could still disappear.

choices.text: It waits until every member has the latest write
choices.why: It did not wait at all; it answered with the majority-committed value.

prompt: What is different when `mongosh` is given `mongodb://mongo1,mongo2,mongo3/shop?replicaSet=rs0` instead of being run `direct` on one container?

choices.text: It finds the primary itself and routes each read by read preference
choices.why: Right: it behaves as a driver does, and the prompt drops `direct`.

choices.text: It writes to all three members at once
choices.why: Writes still go to the primary only.

choices.text: It reads from all three members and returns whatever the majority of them answer
choices.why: A read goes to one member; read concern, not the connection, decides how settled it must be.

choices.text: Nothing, apart from a longer command line
choices.why: The connection to the set is what lets reads follow a read preference.

prompt: Fifteen seconds after `mongo3` was disconnected, it reported itself as `SECONDARY` and refused a write. Who told it to step down?

choices.text: The new primary, which sent it a message over the network telling it to step down
choices.why: The network was exactly what it had lost; no message could reach it.

choices.text: The driver, after the write failed
choices.why: The write failed because it had already stepped down.

choices.text: Nobody: it saw it could reach no majority and stepped down on its own
choices.why: Right. The only member it could reach was itself, one of three.

choices.text: Docker, when the container left the network
choices.why: Docker knows nothing about replica sets; the decision was mongod's.

prompt: Ana's order was inserted on the cut-off `mongo3` with `w: 1` and acknowledged. Which setting would have turned the vanished order into an error she could see?

choices.text: `readConcern: "majority"` on the insert
choices.why: Read concern governs reads; the write would still have been acknowledged by one member.

choices.text: The default write concern, `w: "majority"`
choices.why: Right. Two members could not be reached, so the insert would have waited and then failed when `mongo3` stepped down.

choices.text: A read preference of `nearest` for the application
choices.why: Read preference never affects where a write goes.

choices.text: A shorter election timeout on the three members
choices.why: A shorter timeout narrows the window; any `w: 1` write inside it can still be rolled back.

prompt: After the network was healed, where was Ana's order?

choices.text: In the collection, merged with Bruno's
choices.why: Only Bruno's was there; MongoDB does not merge two histories.

choices.text: Nowhere: a rollback deletes everything it undoes, for good
choices.why: It is kept, which is how `bsondump` could show it.

choices.text: In a BSON file under `/data/db/rollback` on `mongo3`
choices.why: Right, and nothing applies it again unless a person does.

choices.text: In the oplog of `mongo2`, waiting to be replayed when the set is next restarted
choices.why: `mongo2` never received it; it existed only on the losing side.

prompt: Put the partition in the lab in order, from the cut to the rollback.
items: `mongo3` is disconnected while it is primary
`mongo3` misses its heartbeats and steps down
`mongo2` is elected and takes Bruno's order
`mongo3` is reconnected and rolls Ana's order back
trap: Stepping down on one side and electing on the other both wait for the same silence.

prompt: Which of these are true of the three-member set in this lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A write acknowledged by a majority survives the loss of any one member
choices.why: Right: any future primary needs a majority, and any majority holds it.

choices.text: A member cut off from the other two keeps accepting writes until it is reconnected
choices.why: It stepped down within seconds and refused with `not primary`.

choices.text: A read from a secondary can return a value older than the primary's
choices.why: Right: 349.90 against 329.90.

choices.text: The member started first is always the primary
choices.why: The primary changed twice in this lesson; the set elects it.

prompt: A member that wrote operations its new primary never received undoes them when it rejoins. That is called a ___.
hint: The directory `/data/db/` holds a folder of the same name.

prompt: An application reads a customer's basket right after the customer adds an item, and must see that item. Which setting fits?

choices.text: `readPref("secondary")`, to keep load off the primary
choices.why: A secondary can still be behind the write it was just told about.

choices.text: `readPref("nearest")`, since the closest member answers fastest
choices.why: The nearest member may be a secondary that has not applied the write yet.

choices.text: Read from the primary, the default
choices.why: Right, or a causally consistent session; the lesson ran only the first.

choices.text: `readConcern("majority")` on any member
choices.why: Majority buys durability, not freshness; it can return the basket from before the item.
